research_question: How did evolution repurpose ancient primate auditory-vocal circuits into a developmentally organized and partly left-lateralized human speech network, and how do cortical pathways and temporal dynamics support learned vocal control?

primary_direction.name: Phylo-Developmental Speech Circuit Evolution Atlas
primary_direction.thesis: Human speech is best tested as an exaptation-and-reorganization outcome in which ancient primate auditory-vocal circuitry is coupled to human-specialized auditory-motor connectivity, precise laryngeal/oro-facial control, prolonged learning, and developmentally emergent network lateralization.
primary_direction.novelty: A single preregistered atlas connects cross-species representations, developmental lateralization, tract-level connectivity, and speech-related temporal coupling.
predictions: A subset of communication-signal representations will align across humans and nonhuman primates.
Human speech-learning and vocal-control measures will be better explained by auditory-motor connectivity than by activity in any single region.
Leftward language specialization will emerge as a population tendency across development rather than an invariant starting condition.
Speech tasks will show more specific auditory-motor temporal coupling than non-speech auditory or generic oro-facial motor controls.
falsifiers: No cross-species representational alignment above matched non-vocal controls.
Single-region models outperform connection-and-development models after preregistered complexity penalties.
Language lateralization fails to show a developmental trajectory after measurement-error correction.
Speech performance is unrelated to auditory-motor connectivity and dynamic coupling.
